title: Batteries just broke another record in the US
gist: US battery storage hit a record 20.2 GWh in Q2 2026 on cheap batteries and utility-scale and data-center demand, even as residential installs fall on an expired tax credit, while the industry pivots toward domestic manufacturing under new China-content rules and tariffs.

insights.claim: US battery installations hit a new quarterly record in Q2 2026, with 20.2 gigawatt-hours of new capacity coming online — enough to supply the daily electricity needs of about 700,000 homes.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A concrete, verifiable growth metric for the US grid-scale and behind-the-meter battery market that investors in storage, utilities, and grid-hardware suppliers can benchmark against.
insights.locator: Battery installations hit a new record

insights.claim: The pace of installations puts the US on track for 71 gigawatt-hours of new battery capacity in 2026, a 20% increase over 2025.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Gives a full-year growth trajectory for sizing the US energy storage market's near-term demand for cells, inverters, and installation labor.
insights.locator: putting the country on a trajectory to see 71 gigawatt-hours

insights.claim: The growth is being driven by a combination of cheaper batteries and an urgent need for more storage capacity as intermittent renewables like solar and onshore wind are added to the grid.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Ties battery demand growth directly to renewables buildout, making storage a leveraged play on continued solar/wind capacity additions.
insights.locator: This growth is being driven by a combination

insights.claim: An energy storage analyst at BloombergNEF describes batteries as one of the strongest sectors in US energy right now.
insights.speaker: Isshu Kikuma (BloombergNEF), via Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: An independent analyst's characterization that storage is outperforming other US energy subsectors, useful for relative sector allocation.
insights.quote: This is one of the strong sectors in the US.
insights.locator: Overall, batteries are a bright spot in energy right now

insights.claim: Seven new gigascale battery installations (each with more than one gigawatt-hour of capacity) came online in the quarter, and massive utility-scale systems were responsible for most of the record-setting growth.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Shows the record was concentrated in a small number of very large projects rather than broad-based growth, meaning quarter-to-quarter volatility could be high depending on project timing.
insights.quote: It really came down to a handful of big projects.
insights.locator: Massive, utility-scale systems are leading the way

insights.claim: In the behind-the-meter (residential and commercial/industrial) battery category, data centers made up about three-quarters of new commercial-sector battery capacity added.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Directly links the AI/data-center buildout boom to a major new source of battery demand, a cross-sector connection relevant to both energy storage and AI-infrastructure investors.
insights.locator: In the behind-the-meter category, data centers led the way

insights.claim: Residential battery installations are projected to drop 16% in 2026 compared with 2025, a sharp slowdown even as the overall battery market sets records.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: A divergent signal within the storage market: residential-focused battery installers and suppliers face a demand headwind even while utility- and commercial-scale players thrive.
insights.locator: Home installations are projected to drop by 16%

insights.claim: The residential battery slowdown is largely because a federal tax credit that subsidized home battery systems expired in 2025, while tax credits for nonresidential batteries have largely survived; home installations are expected to recover by the end of the decade.
insights.speaker: Shan Tomouk (Benchmark Mineral Intelligence), via Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Identifies a specific, time-bound policy cause (an expired tax credit) for the residential dip, implying it is a temporary demand air-pocket rather than a structural decline.
insights.locator: That drop happened largely because a tax credit

insights.claim: Nearly all battery cells used in current US energy storage installations are still made in China, though some systems are assembled into complete storage units domestically.
insights.speaker: Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Highlights continued US dependence on Chinese battery cells even amid record domestic installation growth, a supply-chain exposure relevant to trade-policy risk.
insights.locator: Today, nearly all the systems coming online use cells made in China

insights.claim: Tariffs and new energy-storage tax-credit rules requiring projects to limit reliance on Chinese-made batteries are pushing the US energy storage industry toward domestic production, but that new domestic manufacturing capacity likely won't be able to meet demand until around 2030, which could push prices up in the meantime.
insights.speaker: Shan Tomouk (Benchmark Mineral Intelligence), via Casey Crownhart
insights.so_what: Flags a multi-year window (through roughly 2030) of potential price pressure and supply tightness for US storage buyers as domestic manufacturing ramps, a timing signal for both battery-cell manufacturers and project developers.
insights.locator: There's a lot of manufacturing capacity set to come online
